title: Five books of prayers
hookLine: the Psalms are in five books, like the Torah, and cover every feeling
last: YOUR BREATH GOES BACK AS PRAISE.

cards: Open a Bible near the middle and you may well land in the Psalms: a hundred and fifty of them.

For a month this path has walked through them: a tree by the water, a cry of my God, my God, a deer at a dry stream, a sparrow at the altar, a weaned child, exiles by the rivers of Babylon, and yesterday, a crash of cymbals.
It can feel like a shuffle playlist: grief, then joy, then fury, then a lullaby. But it isn't a pile. Someone arranged it.

teach.b: The Psalms are divided into five books.

Book one runs from Psalm one to forty-one; book two, forty-two to seventy-two; book three, seventy-three to eighty-nine; book four, ninety to one hundred six; book five, one hundred seven to one hundred fifty.
You can see the seams. The first four books each end with a blessing, like a door closing, and the fifth ends with yesterday's hallelujah.
The first one, in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen."

teach.h: THE PRAYERS OF DAVID ARE ENDED
teach.b: At the end of book two there's a surprising little note: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended." Except they aren't. More psalms of David come later.
Some scholars think that line is left over from an older collection, a sign the book was gathered from earlier collections.
An old Jewish commentary says that as Moses gave Israel five books of the law, David gave them five books of psalms. Inside, every feeling has a place.
Lament runs all through it: complaint, grief, why, how long. Then praise, thanks, pilgrim songs, wisdom, songs for kings.
Athanasius, a bishop of Alexandria, wrote that the other books of the Bible speak to you, but the Psalms speak for you; you find your own soul in them, as in a mirror.

John Calvin later called the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. One more note: Greek and Latin Bibles number most psalms one lower, which is why Catholic and Orthodox prayer books can look off by one.

how: Many Christians pray through the whole book of Psalms regularly: monasteries traditionally chant all 150 every week, and the Book of Common Prayer sets them out to be read through every month.

games.q: you're editing a book of prayers for a whole people. you have joyful songs, angry songs, sad songs. what do you do with the sad ones?
o: cut them, to keep it uplifting.
put them all at the back.
games.why: lament is woven all through the book, right up to its ending in hallelujah.

practice: Ask yourself honestly how you are, tired, grateful, angry, waiting, homesick, and let one of this month's psalms rise that fits: the deer at the dry stream, out of the depths, the weaned child, the new song.
Pick the one that sounds like you, not the one you think you should, and if you pray, pray it.

carryVoice: Your line: every feeling has a psalm. The week ran from the depths to Hannah's weaned child, Babylon, being knit together, everything praising, and hallelujah. That's a whole book, done.
